Wanted but Out of Print: Screening Open Library for Books Entering the Public Domain in 2027¶

Abstract¶

Every 1 January a new group of books loses copyright protection, and publishers who know in advance which of them readers still want can reissue or translate them without a licence. This report asks which books that are free to republish on 1 January 2027, in the United States or in the Philippines, readers still want while publishers no longer supply them. To answer it, the seven files of Open Library's export of 30 September 2022 (47 GiB compressed, including 185.7 million revisions) were parsed with PySpark into Parquet tables, and each of the 26.2 million works was given a rights status under the US publication rule and the Philippine life-plus-50 rule, a demand measure from 4.4 million reading-log entries, and a supply measure from 36.7 million editions. Resolving merged records recovered 5.4% of the shelf entries, and merging duplicate records reduced the catalogue to 24.7 million titles. An estimated 3.10 million titles (12.6%) are already free under at least one rule and 49,675 enter the public domain on 1 January 2027, yet only 87 of the entrants are in high demand, and 68 of those are novels by Agatha Christie, whose whole catalogue becomes free in the Philippines that day without a single Filipino-language edition on record. The 2027 watchlist of high-demand, low-supply entrants has 17 titles, of which a hand check confirmed 13, led by Benjamin Graham's The Intelligent Investor. A Philippine publisher should therefore commission Filipino translations of the most-wanted Christie titles first and verify each watchlist title against primary records before acting, since two of the 17 proved to be false positives caused by errors in the catalogue.

1 Introduction¶

1.1 Background¶

Copyright on a book eventually expires, and from that day the text is in the public domain, which means that anyone may reprint, translate, adapt or digitize it without asking permission or paying a royalty. Expiry comes in yearly batches on 1 January, because copyright terms run to the end of a calendar year (17 U.S.C. § 305; Republic Act No. 8293, 1997, § 214).

Two rules matter for this report, and they release different books. In the United States, a book published before 1978 is protected for at most 95 years from publication (17 U.S.C. § 304), so books first published in 1931 enter the public domain on 1 January 2027 (Hirtle, 2026). The Philippines instead protects a book for the life of its author and fifty years after the author's death (Republic Act No. 8293, 1997, § 213), which frees the works of every author who died in 1976 on that same day. A novel published in 1950 by an author who died in 1960 shows how far the two rules can diverge, since it has been free in the Philippines since 2011 while it can stay protected in the United States until the end of 2045.

1.2 Problem statement¶

Which books that are free to republish on 1 January 2027, in the United States or in the Philippines, do readers still want while publishers no longer supply them?

1.3 Motivation and business value¶

The opportunity is real and it recurs every year. A public-domain text carries no advance, no royalty and no rights negotiation, so a reissue can pay for itself at a print run that a licensed title could not support. Publishers do act on this: in a random sample of new books on sale at Amazon, Heald (2014) found more titles first published in the 1880s than in the 1980s, which shows that books return to print once their copyright ends and stay unavailable while it lasts. Reimers (2019) reached the same conclusion from the 1998 US term extension, finding that copyright significantly limits the availability of books at a cost to readers much larger than the gain to rights holders. Each 1 January therefore opens a new group of books to anyone who is ready for it, on a date that is known decades in advance.

What holds publishers back is selection, since the rights themselves are free. The catalogue used here holds 49,675 titles that enter the public domain on 1 January 2027 under one of the two rules (Section 5.4), and choosing among them means checking when each first appeared, when every author died, whether readers still look for it and whether it is already in print. At a conservative 15 minutes per title, a first pass by hand would take about 12,400 hours, close to seven working years for one editor at 1,800 hours a year. The pipeline in this report makes the same first pass over all 26.2 million works in a few hours of computing, leaving a shortlist short enough for one person to verify in a day.

Three kinds of organization gain from that shortlist.

  • A reprint or trade publisher receives a ranked list of titles with proven reader interest and little recent competition months before they can be sold without a licence, which matters because any competitor may publish the same text from 1 January.
  • A Philippine publisher or translator sees what no US list can show, namely books that are free under the Philippine life-plus-50 rule while still protected in the United States and Europe. Because the catalogue records a Tagalog or Filipino edition for only 1,876 of its 26.2 million works (Section 5.3), translation into Filipino is an almost empty field.
  • A library or digitization programme can use the same ranking to decide which scans to open to the public first, as it orders books by the number of readers waiting for them.

The question needs big-data tooling because it cannot be answered from a sample. A work's first publication year is the minimum over all of its editions and its Philippine status depends on the death year of every one of its authors, while demand is spread thinly over millions of shelf entries. Answering it therefore means joining all 36.7 million edition records, 9.9 million author records and 4.4 million shelf entries, which is why the analysis runs on Apache Spark (Zaharia et al., 2016).

1.4 Objectives and scope¶

  1. Estimate the copyright status of every Open Library work on 1 January 2027 under the US and Philippine rules.
  2. Measure reader demand from reading-log shelves and ratings.
  3. Measure current supply through recent editions, publishers, digitized copies and Filipino-language editions.
  4. Produce a 2027 watchlist of high-demand, low-supply titles that enter the public domain, and a second list of wanted titles that are already free.

The analysis is descriptive, built from counts, shares, joins and aggregations with no predictive model. Every status is an estimate from catalogue metadata and not legal advice, and reader demand is measured among Open Library users as it stood on 30 September 2022.

2 Data Source¶

2.1 Open Library and how its data is collected¶

All data comes from Open Library (https://openlibrary.org), the open, editable book catalogue run by the non-profit Internet Archive. Its stated goal is one web page for every book ever published (Open Library, n.d.-a). The catalogue is built in three ways, and each leaves traces that matter later in this report:

  • Bulk imports of library and trade records. Automated accounts ("bots") load catalogue records from the Library of Congress and other libraries, from booksellers and partners such as Better World Books and Amazon, and from the Internet Archive's own scanning programme (Open Library, n.d.-c). Imports create most records, and they are the reason the same book often exists as several work records.
  • Edits by volunteers. Every record can be edited by any registered user through a wiki interface, and each saved change is kept as a numbered revision (Open Library, n.d.-a). Editors also merge duplicate records; the losing record is kept as a redirect to the survivor.
  • Activity of readers. A logged-in reader can put a book on one of three reading-log shelves (Want to Read, Currently Reading, Already Read) and rate it from one to five stars. These records are public by default (Open Library, n.d.-d) and are published without any user identifier.

Open Library exports the whole database every month as gzip-compressed text files, the "data dumps" (Open Library, n.d.-b). This report uses the seven files of one export (Table 1). Five of them are tab-separated with five columns: record type, key, revision number, time of last change, and the record as JSON. The reading-log and ratings files are plain four-column tables.

Table 1. The seven raw files of the snapshot: what one line holds, how Open Library collects it, and the fields this analysis reads. Sizes are those reported by du (Figure 1); record counts are in Table 4 and Table 7.

File Size One line is How the source collects it Fields used
ol_dump_works 2.4 GiB the current version of one work: a book as an abstract title, across all its editions created by imports and by editors who group editions title, author keys, first publish date, subjects
ol_dump_editions 7.6 GiB the current version of one edition: one published form of a work imported library and bookseller records; user additions work key, publish date, publishers, languages, Internet Archive scan id (ocaid)
ol_dump_authors 430 MiB the current version of one author created with the first imported book of a name; dates come from library records or are typed by editors name, birth date and death date (free text)
ol_dump_reading-log 39 MiB one book on one reader's shelf reader clicks a shelf button; an entry is removed when the reader removes the book work key, shelf, date
ol_dump_ratings 2.8 MiB one star rating by one reader reader clicks a star work key, rating, date
ol_dump (all types) 11 GiB the current version of every record, including redirects and deletions the same database, all record types record type, key, redirect target
ol_cdump (complete) 26 GiB every past revision of every record each saved edit since the catalogue began record type, key, revision, date, author death date

2.2 The snapshot used, and why¶

The course server (Jojie) keeps Open Library exports under /mnt/data/public/openlibrary, one folder per snapshot. The analysis needs the works, editions, authors, reading-log and ratings files together, and Table 2 shows that only the folder 20221007 has them; every other folder holds the revision history alone. That folder is Open Library's export of 30 September 2022, the date of its newest shelf entries and ratings (Table 7), kept in a server folder dated 7 October 2022. All seven of its files are used, 47 GiB in total as reported by du -sch (Figure 1, Table 3); in decimal units this is 50.2 GB.

Two consequences follow from this choice. Demand is measured as it stood in September 2022, more than four years before the date the rights are evaluated for, and the snapshot has no Wikidata file, so author death years come from Open Library alone. Both are discussed as limitations in Section 7.1.

The cell below loads the helper module, starts Spark and locates the snapshot. No raw or processed data is submitted with this report; the notebook rebuilds every table from the files on the server.

def caption(label, text):
    """Display a numbered, self-contained caption for a table or figure."""
    display(HTML(f'<div class="report-caption"><span>{label}.</span> '
                 f'{text}</div>'))


def show(table, label, text, rows=10, index=False, floats=2):
    """Display a caption and the first `rows` rows of a pandas table."""
    caption(label, text)
    if table is None or len(table) == 0:
        print("No rows meet the stated selection criteria.")
        return
    html = table.head(rows).to_html(
        index=index, border=0, na_rep="-",
        float_format=lambda v: f"{v:,.{floats}f}")
    display(HTML('<div class="report-table" style="overflow-x:auto;'
                 'max-width:1100px">' + html + "</div>"))


def show_figure(fig, label, text):
    """Display a matplotlib figure followed by its caption."""
    display(fig)
    plt.close(fig)
    caption(label, text)

3 Methodology Overview¶

Figure 2 shows the pipeline. It answers the problem statement in three phases.

Ingest and explore once. The seven compressed files are parsed with PySpark into eight Parquet tables, keeping only the fields in Table 1. Free-text dates become years. The tables are checked against the raw line counts, described, and profiled for missing values, and keys of merged records are pointed at the record that survived the merge.

Analyse every work. Three independent measures are computed for each of the 26.2 million works and joined into one profile row per work:

  • rights status on 1 January 2027: the first publication year (the earliest edition) gives the US status, and the death year of the last-surviving author gives the Philippine status;
  • demand: how many readers have the work on their Want to Read shelf, with ratings and a 12-month trend;
  • supply: editions published in the last ten years, their publishers, digitized copies and Filipino-language editions.

Select and verify. Duplicate records of the same book are merged into one title. The 2027 watchlist keeps titles that enter the public domain on 1 January 2027, sit in the top 1% of demand and have at most one recent edition; the public-domain list applies the same demand bar to titles that are already free. The published numbers are then recounted along a second code path, the cut-offs are varied, and the estimates for well-known books are compared with facts checked by hand.

4 Methodology¶

All processing code is in helper_code.py, which this notebook imports; every function there has a docstring stating its inputs, outputs and assumptions. The notebook calls those functions in order and discusses what they return. A companion notebook, TEST.ipynb, checks the functions on miniature hand-made dumps whose correct answers were worked out by hand (73 tests, including every copyright boundary year).

4.1 Environment¶

The analysis ran on the course JupyterHub server (Jojie) inside one user allowance of 4 CPU cores and 16 GB of memory, with Python 3.12 and PySpark 4.1.1 in local mode: one Java process acts as driver and executor and runs one task per core. create_spark sets the driver memory to 10 GB, the number of shuffle partitions to 64, the session time zone to UTC and the Parquet codec to zstd. Section 4.11 gives the reasons for these settings and for the other design choices.

To reproduce the report, put FINAL REPORT.ipynb and helper_code.py in one folder on Jojie and choose Kernel > Restart Kernel and Run All Cells. The first run builds the Parquet tables in a parquet/ folder next to the notebook (about 5 GB) and takes two to three hours; later runs reuse them and take about half an hour.

4.2 Ingestion: from compressed text to Parquet¶

Reading. Each file is one gzip stream. A gzip stream can only be decompressed from its first byte, so Spark cannot split it and reads it with a single task, however many cores are free. For the five record dumps, stage_dumps therefore first decompresses each file to plain text in a scratch folder (about 58 GB, deleted afterwards) and counts its lines. Spark splits plain text into 128 MB blocks and parses the blocks in parallel. The all-types dump and the revision history would need more than 200 GB of scratch space as plain text, so build_history_tables reads them straight from gzip, as three concurrent single-task jobs that each reduce their file to a small table while streaming through it. The 27.7 GB revision history took 29 minutes this way.

Parsing. Each line is split on tabs and its JSON column is parsed with an explicit schema that names only the fields in Table 1 (works_schema, editions_schema, authors_schema). Spark then skips every other field while scanning, does not need a first pass to infer types, and returns the same columns for any snapshot. A record whose JSON cannot be parsed is kept with json_ok = False and counted in Table 10, so that a parsing failure cannot pass unnoticed. The parsers apply these rules:

  • Publication years (parse_year): the first four-digit number between 1450 and 2022 in the free-text date, so "February 27, 1997" gives 1997, "c1931" gives 1931 and "19--" gives no year. Years before the spread of printing in Europe or after the snapshot are treated as errors.
  • Birth and death years (parse_life_year): the largest three- or four-digit number in the text, so "1850 or 1851" gives 1851. A later death means longer protection, so an ambiguous date errs towards "still in copyright". Text containing "BC" gives a negative year.
  • Publisher names (normalize_publisher): lower case, punctuation removed and legal suffixes dropped, so that "Penguin Books Ltd." and "Penguin Books" count as one publisher.
  • Shelves and ratings: only the three standard shelves are kept, and a rating outside 1 to 5 becomes null.

Storing. Each table is written once as Parquet with zstd compression. Parquet stores data column by column, so a later step that needs two columns of the editions table reads only those two, in parallel. A table whose folder holds Spark's _SUCCESS marker is reused on later runs, a manifest.json records the snapshot and date constants the tables were built with, and a run with different settings refuses to reuse them.

The cell below runs the ingestion (or reuses its result), and Table 4 compares each table with the line count of its raw file, taken during decompression and therefore independent of Spark. Every line of the five record dumps became exactly one row: nothing was lost in parsing, and this snapshot contains no shelf entry or rating that the parsers reject.

In [5]:
start = time.time()
# Parse the five record dumps once (decompress, then parse in parallel);
# a table whose Parquet folder is complete is reused on later runs.
parquet_paths = helper.build_parquet_tables(spark, dumps, PARQUET_DIR)
# Reduce the all-types dump (record-type census, merged-key redirects)
# and the revision history, read straight from gzip.
history_paths = helper.build_history_tables(spark, DATA_DIR, PARQUET_DIR)
raw_tables = helper.load_tables(spark, {**parquet_paths, **history_paths})
print(f"Ingestion step finished in {time.time() - start:,.0f} s "
      "(the first run takes two to three hours).")
parquet_gb = sum(helper._folder_size(p) for p in
                 {**parquet_paths, **history_paths}.values()) / 1e9
print(f"Parquet tables on disk: {parquet_gb:.2f} GB, from "
      f"{raw_gib:.1f} GiB of compressed input")
show(helper.ingestion_check(raw_tables, PARQUET_DIR), "Table 4",
     "Ingestion check: lines in each raw record dump (counted while "
     "decompressing, independently of Spark) against rows in its "
     "Parquet table, and the share of lines kept.")

The all-types dump gives a second, independent check. It holds the current version of every key, so the live works, editions and authors in it must equal the rows parsed from the three separate dumps. Table 5 confirms that they match exactly. The same table shows how much the catalogue is curated: 485,432 work keys (1.8% of the work namespace) and 349,457 author keys (3.4%) are redirects left behind by merges, and 1.24 million edition keys have been deleted. Table 6 lists the record types; works, editions and authors make up 96.2% of the file.

4.3 Data exploration¶

Table 7 describes each of the seven raw datasets with a few simple statistics, and Table 8 and Table 9 break down the two reader datasets. The points that shape the rest of the analysis are these.

  • Works and editions. The catalogue has 26.2 million works and 36.7 million editions. A work has 1.32 editions on average and the median work has one, while the largest has 3,760: supply is very unevenly spread. The median edition was published in 1996, and 19.6% of editions date from 2013 or later, the ten-year window this report calls "recent".
  • Authors. Of 9.9 million author records, 14.9% have a usable birth year and only 3.8% a usable death year. Where a death year is known its median is 1915, so the dated authors are mostly long dead. Section 4.4 investigates this gap, because the Philippine rule depends on it.
  • Reading log. 4.36 million shelf entries cover 1.43 million distinct works, 5.5% of the catalogue. 82.9% of entries are Want to Read (Table 8), which makes this shelf the natural demand measure: it records books that readers intend to read and may not yet have. Entries run from 27 October 2017 to 30 September 2022.
  • Ratings. 291,305 ratings cover 155,041 works. They are skewed to the top: 44.8% are five stars and the mean is 4.00 (Table 9), so a rating says little about relative demand and is used only as a secondary signal.
  • All-types dump and revision history. The all-types dump has 75.6 million records of 31 types. The revision history has 185.7 million revisions from 19 March 2008 to 30 September 2022; 40.8% of them created a record and the rest are edits, and 13.1 million concern authors.

4.4 Missing values and merged records¶

How much is missing. Table 10 gives, for every field the analysis uses, the share of rows where it is present and usable. Table 11 confirms that no work, edition or author key occurs twice, so no join can double-count a record. Three gaps are large enough to change results, and each was investigated before deciding how to treat it (Table 13 to Table 16).

  1. Works without their own first-publish date (83.0%). This is how the catalogue is designed, not damage: the date of a book lives on its editions, and the work-level field is filled only occasionally. Table 15 shows that an edition supplies a year for 80.1% of works, so 97.0% of works can be dated. The remaining 2.97% (works whose editions are undated, or that have no edition) are left undated and reported as "unknown". No year is imputed, because any imputed year would assign a legal status.

  2. Authors without a death year (96.2%). Table 13 shows that the gap is far from random. It is almost complete for authors with no birth year either (99.7% missing; these are 88.2% of all authors without a death year) and for authors born in 1940 or later (99.0% missing), most of whom were alive in 2022. It shrinks to 54.9% for authors born 1850-1899 and to 11.3% for those born before 1850. The revision history explains the first group: Table 14 shows that 79.7% of authors without a death year were never edited after the import that created them, against 34.0% of authors who have one. A missing death year therefore means "an imported name that nobody has looked at" or "still alive", and neither can safely be read as "died long ago". Death years are not imputed: a work receives a Philippine status only if every one of its authors has a death year, and is otherwise reported as "unknown". Section 4.6 tests one cautious alternative, treating authors born before 1850 as certainly dead.

  3. Editions without a link to a work (6.0%). Table 16 shows that these 2.2 million editions are otherwise ordinary records (91.0% are dated) but only 0.6% have a scan, against 15.0% of linked editions. They are records that were imported and never grouped into a work. They cannot be attributed to any work, so they are excluded from the first-year and supply measures, which makes supply a lower bound.

Two smaller gaps need no action: 39.4% of shelf entries carry no edition key (the analysis works at the level of the work), and 14.2% of editions have no language (they simply cannot count as Filipino editions).

Merged records. A fourth kind of missing value is invisible in a coverage table: a key that is present but points to a record that no longer exists under that key. When editors merge two work records, shelf entries and ratings logged against the losing key keep that key, and in a plain join with the works table they silently disappear. The redirects in the all-types dump repair this. resolve_redirect_chains follows each redirect to its final target (a record can be merged more than once), and resolve_merged_keys rewrites the work key of every edition, shelf entry and rating and the author keys of every work. Table 12 shows the effect: 5.4% of all shelf entries and 8.4% of all ratings would have been lost without this step, far more than the 1.8% share of merged keys suggests, because the records that editors bother to merge are the popular ones. After the repair 0.05% of shelf entries still point to no live work (their work was deleted) and are dropped. The remaining sections use the repaired tables.

4.5 Author death years and their history¶

reconcile_author_deaths attaches one birth year and one death year to every author, using the parsing rule of Section 4.2. Open Library can also take death dates from Wikidata, but this snapshot contains no Wikidata file (only 1.7% of its authors carry a Wikidata identifier), so every year comes from Open Library's own text. An author whose death year is earlier than the birth year, or more than 120 years after it, is marked life_dates_conflict.

Because the Philippine status of a book rests on a single number typed into an author record, the revision history was used to ask how those numbers came about and how stable they are. death_year_history traces each current author through all of its revisions (Figure 3, Table 17).

  • Death years arrived with the imports. Of the 371,342 authors who have a death year today, 73.6% already had it in 2008, the year of the first bulk imports, and only 25,427 (6.8%) received it in a later edit. For the authors who died in 1976, the group that enters the public domain in the Philippines in 2027, 76.1% of death years were recorded in 2008.
  • Coverage is falling. The share of authors with a death year was 4.5% in 2008 and is 3.8% in 2022, because 2.98 million author records were created from 2019 to 2022, nearly all without dates. Newer snapshots will not close the gap by themselves.
  • Recorded years are stable. Only 453 authors (0.12% of those with a death year) have ever had a different death year in an earlier revision, and for only 58 would the Philippine status have differed. The risk in the Philippine estimates is therefore missing years and wrong author links, not years that change after they are entered.

4.6 Rights status¶

Each work receives a status as of 1 January 2027 under the rules in Table 18, implemented in us_status and life_plus_status and applied to all works by estimate_copyright_status.

Table 18. The copyright rules applied, as they stand on 1 January 2027. Y is the year of first publication and D the death year of the last-surviving author. Sources: 17 U.S.C. §§ 302-305 and Hirtle (2026) for the United States; Republic Act No. 8293 (1997), §§ 213-214, for the Philippines.

Regime Basis Public domain already Enters on 1 Jan 2027 Not free, or not known
United States Y; at most 95 years for works published before 1978 Y ≤ 1930 Y = 1931 1932-1963: free only if the copyright was not renewed ("renewal unknown"); 1964 onwards: protected
Philippines D; life + 50 years, counted from 1 January after the death D ≤ 1975 D = 1976 D ≥ 1977: protected; any author without a death year, or no author: unknown
Life + 70 (EU, UK and many other countries), for comparison only D; life + 70 years D ≤ 1955 D = 1956 D ≥ 1957: protected

Three points about these rules affect how the results should be read.

  • A 1931 book whose US copyright was not renewed in its 28th year is free already; 1 January 2027 is the latest date on which any 1931 book becomes free (Hirtle, 2026).
  • For 1932-1963 the renewal decides, and renewal records are not in Open Library. A New York Public Library analysis of the Catalog of Copyright Entries found that about 25% of the book copyrights registered from 1923 to 1964 were renewed (New York Public Library, 2019), so most of this group is probably free, but the data cannot say which works.
  • The Philippine rule needs the death year of every author, and the last survivor counts (Republic Act No. 8293, 1997, § 213.2).

A work's first-publication year is the earlier of its own first_publish_date and its earliest dated edition. This is also how Open Library reports "first published", but it makes the estimate sensitive to a single wrong date, so two checks are attached to every work:

  • year_before_birth: the first year is earlier than the last author's birth year plus 10, which no real first edition can be. Together with author_dates_conflict (Section 4.5) this makes a work flagged; flagged works stay in the catalogue counts but are excluded from both lists.
  • gap_after_death: the first year is more than 70 years after the last author's death. This is a warning, not an exclusion. It fires for classics whose early editions are not catalogued, and also for modern books attached to the record of a much older namesake.

A work is potentially public domain if it is unflagged and public domain under the US rule or the Philippine rule, and it enters in 2027 if it is unflagged and enters under either rule (Table 19).

4.7 Demand¶

compute_demand counts, for every work, the entries on each shelf and the valid ratings. The Want to Read count is the demand measure: it is by far the largest signal (Section 4.3) and the only one that records an unmet intention. For trends it also counts the Want-to-Read entries logged in the 12 months to 30 September 2022 and in the 12 months before.

One property of the data limits what trends can show. The dump holds only entries that are still on a shelf: when a reader finishes a book and moves it to Already Read, the Want-to-Read entry is gone. Older months are therefore undercounted, and a rising line partly reflects this survivorship and the growth of the site. The results compare rights groups with each other and do not read the slope itself as growing interest.

4.8 Supply and the work profile¶

compute_supply summarizes the editions of each work:

  • editions and recent editions, those published from 2013 to 2022, the ten years up to the snapshot. A wanted work with no recent edition is an opening; one that many publishers keep reissuing is already served;
  • publishers and recent publishers, counted on normalized names;
  • digitized copies, editions with an Internet Archive scan, which show that a source text is at hand;
  • Filipino-language editions, editions catalogued with the language code tgl (Tagalog) or fil (Filipino).

An edition without a valid year counts as an edition but never as recent, so recent counts are lower bounds. build_work_profile joins status, demand and supply into one row per work, with zeros for works that nobody has shelved or that have no linked edition.

Duplicate records. Bulk imports often create several work records for one book, each holding part of its editions and shelf entries. A single record then understates both the demand for the book and its supply, and the lists would show the same book several times. consolidate_titles merges work records that have the same normalized title (lower case, punctuation and a leading article removed) and exactly the same set of authors. Requiring identical authors keeps the merge conservative: it cannot join different books by different people, at the price of leaving apart duplicates whose titles differ, for example by a subtitle. Counts are summed, the first year is the earliest of the merged records, and the US status and flags are recomputed from it. The catalogue statistics in Sections 5.1 to 5.3 describe work records, the unit of the catalogue; the two lists are built on titles. Table 20 shows what the merge changes.

In [13]:
# Join status, demand and supply per work, then merge duplicate records.
demand = helper.compute_demand(tables["reading_log"], tables["ratings"])
supply = helper.compute_supply(tables["editions"])
profile = helper.materialize(
    spark, helper.build_work_profile(status, demand, supply),
    PARQUET_DIR / "work_profile",
)
titles = helper.materialize(
    spark, helper.consolidate_titles(profile),
    PARQUET_DIR / "title_profile",
)
print(f"Work profile: {profile.count():,} work records x "
      f"{len(profile.columns)} columns")
show(helper.consolidation_summary(profile, titles), "Table 20",
     "Effect of merging duplicate work records: records, titles after "
     "the merge, records absorbed into another row, titles built from "
     "several records, the largest such title, and the share of all "
     "Want-to-Read entries that sit on merged titles.")

4.9 Data filtering and the two lists¶

Rows leave the analysis at five points before any list is built, and Table 21 states the rule, the reason and the number of rows at each of them. None of these steps removes a work from the catalogue counts, since a work with a missing value keeps its row and is reported in an "unknown" group.

Table 21. Filtering steps applied before the lists, with the rows affected and the share kept. Counts come from Table 4, Table 10, Table 16, Table 12 and Table 22.

Step Rule and reason Rows affected Kept
1. Parsing keep only the record type of each dump, the three standard shelves, and rows with a work key, since anything else is not a book, a shelf entry or a rating 0 of 77.4 million lines 100%
2. Dates a date text with no year from 1450 to 2022 gives a null year, because an impossible year would produce a false rights status 101,996 of 35,641,389 edition dates; 28,999 of 400,341 author death dates 99.7% of edition dates; 92.8% of death dates
3. Edition-work link an edition that names no work cannot be attributed, so it is left out of first-year and supply measures 2,195,728 of 36,657,084 editions 94.0%
4. Deleted records after merged keys are resolved, a row that still points to no live work is dropped, as its work no longer exists 2,169 of 4,355,023 shelf entries; 278 of 291,305 ratings; 84 editions 99.95% of shelf entries; 99.90% of ratings
5. Flagged titles a title with an impossible first year or impossible author dates stays in the counts but cannot enter a list, because its status rests on a known error 31,446 of 24,686,637 titles 99.87%

The two lists are then cut from the title table by the steps in Table 22, each applied on top of the one before.

  1. Enters the public domain on 1 January 2027 under the US rule (first published 1931) or the Philippine rule (last author died 1976). This is the question's own condition, and it keeps 49,675 titles, 0.20% of the unflagged ones.
  2. High demand: a Want-to-Read count at or above the 99th percentile among titles that have at least one entry, which is 28 entries. The percentile is taken among shelved titles because 95% of titles have no entry at all, so a percentile over every title would be zero. This step keeps 87 titles, 0.18% of the entrants.
  3. Low supply: at most one edition published from 2013 to 2022. One edition is allowed so that a single reprint does not hide a title that the market has otherwise left alone. This step keeps 17 of the 87 titles (19.5%), and they form the 2027 watchlist.

The public-domain list applies the same demand bar to the 3,101,791 unflagged titles that are already free under either rule, which leaves 1,139 titles (0.04%). Both lists are ranked by Want-to-Read entries, then by entries in the last 12 months, then by number of ratings. Because the two cut-offs are judgement calls, Section 5.4 reports the size of the watchlist under other choices.

In [14]:

4.10 Validation¶

Three checks guard the numbers in this report, each aimed at a different kind of error.

Recounts. An aggregation over tens of millions of rows can go wrong silently when a join drops or duplicates rows, so validate_analysis recomputes key totals along a second code path and compares the two answers (Table 23). The editions attached to known works, for example, are counted directly from the editions table and compared with the sum of the per-work edition counts, and the Python versions of the US and Philippine rules are applied to a random 0.1% sample of works to confirm that Spark assigned the same status. All ten recounts match.

Unit tests. TEST.ipynb runs the helper functions on miniature dumps with planted traps, such as malformed JSON, a redirect, a custom shelf and an out-of-range rating, and it checks every Spark expression against a pure-Python twin of the same rule.

Hand-checked audit. Recounts show that the code does what it says, but they cannot show that the catalogue is right. audit_estimates therefore compares the estimated status of 28 well-known, high-demand works with the status implied by first-publication and death years checked by hand (Table 24, Table 25). The sample is deliberately made of famous books, which a reader of the lists would act on first, so it does not estimate the error rate of the whole catalogue. Its result is clear all the same: the Philippine status was never wrong where the data allowed one (19 correct, 5 left unknown for lack of a death year), whereas the US status was wrong for 6 of the 27 works that had one, always because the earliest catalogued edition is not the true first edition. The Philippine estimate fails by saying "unknown", which is safe, while the US estimate can fail by naming the wrong year, and that is why every list in Section 5 is presented as a shortlist to verify.

In [15]:

4.11 Design constraints and alternatives¶

The pipeline had to run inside one user allowance on a shared server (4 CPU cores, 16 GB of memory, a shared scratch disk) and to rest on catalogue data with known gaps. Table 26 lists the choices this forced, the reason for each, and the alternative that was weighed against it. Where a table is cited the alternative was computed and its effect is reported in Section 5, and where the row says "not computed" the alternative was rejected on the stated reasoning alone.

Table 26. Design decisions, the constraint behind each, and the alternative considered.

Decision Constraint and reason Alternative considered
Decompress the five record dumps to plain text before parsing gzip cannot be split, so Spark would parse each file with one of the four cores; plain text splits into 128 MB blocks that all cores parse at once reading the .gz files directly needs no scratch disk but ties the 8 GB editions file to a single task
Read the all-types dump and the revision history straight from gzip as plain text they would exceed 200 GB on a shared scratch disk; each job only filters and reduces, so one streaming task per file is enough (29 minutes for the largest) staging them too would parallelize the parse at a disk cost the server cannot guarantee
Explicit JSON schemas with only the needed fields with 16 GB of memory, wide records cannot be held whole; a declared schema also avoids an inference pass over 58 GB schema inference reads every file twice and returns hundreds of columns that are never used
Spark expressions with tested pure-Python twins, and no Python UDFs a UDF sends every row to a Python worker and back, which is slow on 36.7 million rows; built-in expressions stay inside the JVM UDFs would let each rule be written once, at a cost in run time
Parquet files for intermediate tables in place of cache() Spark is lazy, so every later count would redo the joins; cached tables of 26 million rows do not fit in memory next to a shuffle, and files survive a kernel restart in-memory caching is simpler but competes with shuffles for the same 10 GB heap
Broadcast join for the redirect table the table has under a million rows, so sending it to every task avoids shuffling 36.7 million editions a sort-merge join would shuffle and sort both sides
64 shuffle partitions the default of 200 creates many tiny tasks on four cores, while 64 gives partitions of about 400,000 work rows fewer partitions risk running out of memory in the widest aggregations
The snapshot of September 2022 it is the only one on the server with all five record dumps (Table 2) later snapshots hold only the revision history, from which shelves and ratings cannot be rebuilt
First year = earliest edition this is Open Library's own definition, and the only source for the 83% of works without their own date the second-earliest edition year, which ignores a lone early date (Table 29)
No imputation of death years a guessed death year would grant or deny a legal status (Table 13) treating authors born before 1850 as certainly dead (Table 30)
Philippine term of life + 50 years the term in force (Republic Act No. 8293, 1997, § 213) life + 70 years, the term of the EU and UK (Table 27)
Demand bar at the 99th percentile; supply bar at one recent edition a list must be short enough to verify by hand the 90th and 95th percentiles and bars of 0, 2 and 5 editions (Table 38)
Lists built on merged titles duplicate records split the demand and supply of one book (Table 20) lists on raw work records, which repeat the same book (computed in Section 5.4)
Titles merged only on the same title and the same set of authors a merge must never join different books, since that would invent demand merging on the title alone or on similar titles would catch more duplicates but would also join unrelated books; not computed
Want to Read as the demand measure it holds 82.9% of shelf entries and is the only shelf that records an intention not yet met (Table 8) adding Currently Reading and Already Read would count demand that is already satisfied, and ratings cover only 155,041 works; not computed
"Recent" supply = editions of 2013 to 2022 ten years is short enough to mean "available now" and long enough that one uncatalogued year does not hide a reissue a five-year window would count fewer editions as recent and so lengthen the lists; not computed
Valid publication years 1450 to 2022 printing with movable type in Europe begins about 1450, and a year after the snapshot is impossible no lower bound would accept typing errors such as three-digit years read as dates
Flag margins: first year before birth + 10; warning at 70 years after death no author publishes before the age of ten, and 70 years is the longest term considered here a wider birth margin would catch more mis-dated editions but would also exclude genuine early works; not computed

5 Results and Discussion¶

5.1 How much of the catalogue is free, or will be¶

Under the US rule, 2.58 million works (9.8%) were first published in 1930 or earlier and are already in the public domain, while 37,780 (0.14%) date from 1931 and enter on 1 January 2027 (Figure 4, Table 27). A further 1.68 million (6.4%) fall in the 1932-1963 window, where most copyrights were probably never renewed but the data cannot say which. The catalogue is dominated by recent publishing, with 70.5% of works first published in 1978 or later.

The Philippine rule gives a different picture, and missing data is the main reason. Because 85.7% of works have an author without a death year and 4.5% have no author at all, only 9.8% of works can be classified. Most of those are already free (2.06 million works, 7.9% of the catalogue), 482,148 are protected, and 16,270 enter in 2027. Under life plus 70 years, shown for comparison, the free group would shrink by 308,809 works to 1.75 million, which is the size of the advantage that the shorter Philippine term gives a local publisher.

The two rules free different books, as the cross-tabulation in Table 28 shows. About 0.94 million works are public domain in the Philippines without being so under the US rule, among them 276,571 from the renewal-unknown years and 444,520 first catalogued in 1978 or later, which are mostly late editions and translations of authors who died long ago. The reverse case is rare, since only 6,349 works published by 1930 remain protected in the Philippines through an author who died after 1976. Taken together, 3.50 million work records (13.3%) are potentially public domain under at least one rule (Table 19).

How far these counts can be trusted depends on the first-publication year, and Figure 5 shows two artefacts in it. Works dated exactly 1900 are more than twice as many as in the neighbouring years, and those dated 1800 nearly four times as many as in 1801, a pattern that points to placeholder dates in some imported catalogues. Both spikes lie before 1931, so if the true dates are later the US public-domain group is somewhat overstated. The peak in the last years of the chart has a different cause, as it reflects the bulk imports of recent books seen in Figure 3.

The data-quality flags and two tests of alternative assumptions put numbers on the remaining doubt.

  • Flags. 25,716 works have a first year earlier than their author's birth plus ten years and 8,219 have authors with impossible life dates (Table 19); these are excluded from both lists. Another 496,508 works carry the gap_after_death warning, most of them classics whose early editions were never catalogued.
  • A more cautious first year. If a lone earliest edition date is ignored and the second-earliest year is used for works with three or more distinct edition years, 24,701 works (0.96%) leave the US public-domain group and 1,029 (2.7%) leave the 1931 group (Table 29). Among the 1,525 works of 1931 that could be tested, two in three would move, so for a book with many editions a single date decides the estimate. This is an upper bound on the error, since a true first edition followed by later reprints moves as well.
  • A less cautious death rule. Treating authors born before 1850 as certainly dead would move 69,089 works from "unknown" to public domain in the Philippines, 0.31% of the unknown group (Table 30), and 33,392 of them are not already free under the US rule. The strict baseline therefore gives up very little.

5.2 Reader demand¶

Older works are shelved less often, but they are far from forgotten. Only 2.3% of US public-domain works have a Want-to-Read entry against 5.5% of works published since 1978 (Table 31), yet works first published before 1964 still hold 454,658 entries, 12.6% of all demand. Readers who do find an older book rate it as highly as a new one, since the mean rating lies between 3.7 and 4.0 stars in every group, so age alone is no sign of weak interest.

The trend in Figure 6 has to be read with care. All four rights groups rise and fall together: a peak in the spring of 2020, which coincides with the first pandemic lockdowns, is followed by a second climb through 2022 that ends at the highest values of the series. Because the dump keeps only entries that are still on a shelf, the most recent months have lost the fewest entries and would look strongest even with constant interest. Comparing groups is safer than reading the slope, and it shows no shift towards older books: entries in the last 12 months grew by 88% for public-domain works and by 99% for works since 1978, which leaves the public-domain share of new entries flat at about 4.5%. Demand for free books is thus a steady fraction of a growing total, and nothing in the data suggests that it will fade before 2027.

5.3 Current supply¶

Older works are almost never reissued, according to the catalogue. Only 1.5% of US public-domain works, 1.1% of the 1931 works and 0.8% of the 1932-1963 works have an edition dated 2013 or later, against 27.0% of works published since 1978 (Figure 7, Table 32). The source text is often at hand all the same, because 51.9% of public-domain works have an Internet Archive scan, although that share falls to 17.3% for the 1931 works that are about to become free.

Filipino-language editions are close to absent. In the whole catalogue only 1,876 works have an edition catalogued in Tagalog or Filipino, which is 0.007% of works and never more than 0.01% in any rights group. Open Library certainly under-records Philippine publishers, so the true number is higher, but a gap of this size cannot be explained by cataloguing alone.

Wanted books with no recent edition exist, though they are not the most famous ones. Table 33 crosses demand with recent supply for the titles that are free or about to be. Of the 235 titles with at least 100 Want-to-Read entries, 134 have ten or more recent editions and are crowded markets, whereas 44 have none. One step lower, among titles with 10 to 99 entries, 2,344 have no recent edition, so the unserved demand sits in the middle of the distribution, below the classics that every publisher already prints.

5.4 The 2027 opportunity and the watchlist¶

Who enters. 49,675 unflagged titles enter the public domain on 1 January 2027, of which 35,550 do so through the US rule alone, 14,052 through the Philippine rule alone and 73 through both (Table 34). Almost none of them is in print, as 98.0% have no edition since 2013, but almost none is wanted either, since only 5.0% have a single Want-to-Read entry. Demand is therefore the criterion that selects, and the Philippine entrants carry most of it, with 10,773 entries against 3,080 for the US entrants although they are fewer than half as many.

The demand belongs to one author. Of the 87 entrants in high demand, 78 enter through the Philippine rule and 68 are books by Agatha Christie, who died on 12 January 1976 (Table 35, Table 36). Her 973 catalogued titles hold 7,039 Want-to-Read entries, half of all demand among the 2027 entrants, and not one of them has a Filipino-language edition on record. Her best-known novels are well supplied in English, which keeps them off the low-supply watchlist, so for a Philippine publisher the opening lies in translation and not in reprinting. Outside the Philippines the same books stay protected for years, until 2047 under life plus 70 and for 95 years from publication in the United States.

The watchlist. Seventeen titles combine high demand with at most one recent edition (Figure 8, Table 37). Every one of them was checked by hand against biographical and library records, and the check column of Table 37 records the outcome.

  • Thirteen are confirmed. Nine enter through the Philippine rule, led by Benjamin Graham's The Intelligent Investor (935 entries across five duplicate records, none with an edition since 2013), followed by three Christie titles, Carl Boyer's history of the calculus, Auntie Mame, J. Paul Getty's How to Be Rich, Lord Kinross's The Ottoman Centuries and Paul Gallico's Flowers for Mrs. Harris. Four enter through the US rule as 1931 first editions: Joy of Cooking, Industrial Accident Prevention, Alfred Adler's What Life Should Mean to You and The Epic of America.
  • Two are false positives, and both come from the catalogue. Security Analysis is credited to Graham alone, although his co-author David Dodd died in 1988, and Margarete Bieber's death is recorded as 1976 when she died in 1978. Neither book is free in 2027.
  • One is already free, since Saussure's Cours de linguistique générale appeared in 1916 and only its 1931 edition is catalogued, and one needs care, because the "Miss Marple" record mixes several omnibus volumes.

Two cautions apply even to the confirmed titles. Only the original text becomes free, so the 1931 Joy of Cooking and the 1949 Intelligent Investor may be reprinted while their later revisions and commentaries may not. And "no recent edition" describes the catalogue of 2022, so current availability has to be checked before any investment.

The cut-offs change the length of the list, not its nature. Lowering the demand bar to the 95th percentile (8 entries) gives 128 titles and the 90th percentile (4 entries) gives 307, while allowing up to five recent editions at the 99th percentile gives 40 (Table 38). Merging duplicate records matters more than either threshold: on raw work records the same procedure returns 25 rows in which The Intelligent Investor appears as separate entries, each understating its demand.

5.5 Wanted books that are already free¶

The most-wanted free books are free in the Philippines only. The public-domain list holds 1,139 titles, and its top is led by books whose US status is "renewal unknown" while their authors died more than fifty years ago (Table 39): Think and Grow Rich (Napoleon Hill, died 1970; 2,789 entries), Nineteen Eighty-Four and Animal Farm (Orwell, died 1950), The Hobbit (Tolkien, died 1973), Brave New World (Huxley, died 1963) and Le Petit Prince (Saint-Exupéry, died 1944). These are crowded markets with dozens of recent editions each, although none of those shown has more than one Filipino edition on record.

The low-supply view gives the less obvious leads. Requiring at most one recent edition leaves 584 titles (Table 40). Those that survive a hand check of their authors include Napoleon Hill's How to Raise Your Own Salary (312 entries, one edition), Edgar Payne's Composition of Outdoor Painting (228), Maria Montessori's The Secret of Childhood (143) and, of particular interest for a Philippine publisher, Emilio Aguinaldo's memoir Mga Gunita ng Himagsikan. Aguinaldo died in 1964, so the memoir has been free in the Philippines since 2015, and the catalogue holds a single edition of it from 1998 against 172 readers who want it.

The same table shows how the estimates fail, and each failure has a recognisable signature.

  • A wrong first year. Atlas Shrugged (1957) is dated 1920 through one mis-dated edition and so appears free in the US.
  • A missing co-author. Goodnight Moon lists its writer and omits its illustrator, who died in 1988.
  • A wrong author link. Predictions of Nostradamus about the Philippines (1995) is attached to Nostradamus himself. This case is caught by the gap_after_death warning, which fires on 7.0% of the public-domain list and on none of the 87 high-demand entrants (Table 41).
  • Misplaced demand. Alice in Wonderland in Five Acts, a record with one edition, holds 864 entries and none from the last 12 months, which suggests entries meant for Alice's Adventures in Wonderland.

6 Conclusion¶

The question was which books that are free to republish on 1 January 2027, in the United States or in the Philippines, readers still want while publishers no longer supply them. The data gives a specific answer.

  • Entering in 2027 and under-supplied: 17 titles, 13 of them confirmed. Out of 49,675 titles that enter the public domain, 87 are in high demand and 17 of those have at most one edition since 2013. The confirmed titles are led by The Intelligent Investor (free in the Philippines) and the 1931 first edition of Joy of Cooking (free in the United States).
  • Entering in 2027 and wanted, but supplied only in English: the Agatha Christie catalogue. Christie accounts for 68 of the 87 high-demand entrants and half of all demand among entrants, and none of her 973 titles has a Filipino edition on record. This is the largest single opportunity in the data, and it exists only under Philippine law.
  • Already free and under-supplied: 584 titles, most of them free under the Philippine rule alone, with Aguinaldo's Mga Gunita ng Himagsikan as the clearest Philippine example.

The answer is firm in its counts and provisional in its individual titles. Every total was reproduced along a second code path, and the hand checks found the Philippine status reliable wherever it could be computed. They also found that one US status in five was wrong among famous books and that two of the 17 watchlist titles were false positives, so the lists are shortlists for verification and not rights clearances.

7 Limitations and Recommendations¶

7.1 Limitations¶

The snapshot is from September 2022. Rights are evaluated for 2027, but demand and supply are those of more than four years earlier, the latest date for which the server holds shelves and ratings. A title that was out of print in 2022 may have been reissued since, and interest may have moved, which is why the first recommendation is to check current availability.

Death years are missing for 96% of authors. As a result 86% of works have no Philippine status, and the Philippine counts are lower bounds on what is really free. The gap is structural, since Section 4.5 showed that death years arrived with the imports of 2008 and that coverage has fallen since, and the snapshot has no Wikidata file from which to fill it.

The catalogue's links are sometimes wrong. A missing co-author (Security Analysis), a wrong death year (Bieber) or a namesake (Nostradamus) each turns a protected book into an apparent opportunity. No rule can detect a missing co-author, because the record looks complete, so these errors surface only when a title is checked by hand.

The first-publication year is the earliest catalogued edition. It can be too early through a mis-dated edition, too late where early editions are missing (496,508 works), or a placeholder such as 1900. Section 5.1 bounds the effect at about 1% of the public-domain group, but the audit shows that it concentrates in famous books with many editions.

US law is applied in its simplest form. Renewal records are not in the data, so 1.68 million works from 1932-1963 stay unresolved, and the rule ignores works published without a copyright notice, works of the US government, and foreign works whose US copyright was restored in 1996. For the Philippines only the general life-plus-50 term is applied, without the separate terms for anonymous works and without the rights of translators and editors in a particular edition.

Work records are not books. Merging records with the same title and authors removed 1.5 million duplicates, yet records whose titles differ by a subtitle remain apart, and a work bundles revised editions and compilations whose new material may still be protected. Supply measured on such records is a lower bound.

Demand is that of Open Library users. They are not a sample of all readers and certainly not of Philippine readers, and the reading log keeps only current shelf entries, which undercounts older interest.

7.2 Recommendations¶

For a Philippine publisher

  1. Commission Filipino translations of the most-wanted Christie novels for release from 1 January 2027. Table 35 ranks them: And Then There Were None, Murder on the Orient Express, The A.B.C. Murders, The Murder of Roger Ackroyd and Death on the Nile. Translation should start from the original English text, and distribution should stay within the Philippines, because the books remain protected elsewhere.
  2. Reissue the confirmed Philippine-rule titles of the watchlist, starting with The Intelligent Investor in its 1949 or 1973 text, and consider the titles that are already free and under-supplied, above all Mga Gunita ng Himagsikan.
  3. Verify before investing. For each title, confirm the first edition in a national bibliography, confirm every author, illustrator and translator and their death dates, check that the edition used is the original text, and check current availability with booksellers. The watchlist is short enough for one person to clear in a day, and Table 37 already records the outcome for this snapshot.

For a US reprint publisher

  1. Prepare the four confirmed 1931 first editions (Joy of Cooking, Industrial Accident Prevention, What Life Should Mean to You, The Epic of America), and treat the 1931 group as thin: its 35,550 titles carry only 3,080 Want-to-Read entries in total.

For Open Library and its data

  1. Add death dates to the most-shelved authors first. A few hundred edits to the authors of the 12,738 high-demand titles would classify far more reader demand than any bulk import, since coverage is limited by unedited records and not by unstable ones.

Future work

  1. Resolve the renewal-unknown group. Matching the 1.68 million works of 1932-1963 against the digitized renewal records of the Catalog of Copyright Entries would turn the largest uncertain group into firm answers, and it is the most valuable extension of this pipeline.
  2. Add Wikidata death dates and a current snapshot. Open Library now publishes a Wikidata dump (Open Library, n.d.-b), and helper_code.py already reads it when the file is present, so a newer export would raise Philippine coverage and replace the 2022 demand figures.
  3. Reuse the method elsewhere. The reference date and the term are two constants, so the same code yields the 2028 watchlist (works of 1932, deaths in 1977) or the list for any country with a life-based term. The steps that mattered most here, resolving merged keys and merging duplicate records before counting, apply to any analysis built on a community-edited catalogue.
